findings.title: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme — drinking water service levels
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — The JMP maintains the official national and sub-national ladder for drinking-water service levels in Kenya, distinguishing safely managed, basic, limited, unimproved and surface-water use. Peri-urban settlements around Lake Victoria are the kind of setting where the JMP ladder typically separates piped-network households from neighbours still relying on limited or surface sources.

findings.title: BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas — Kenya hydrogeology
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — The British Geological Survey's Africa Groundwater Atlas describes Kenya's aquifer environments, including the weathered and fractured basement and the sedimentary and volcanic units of the Lake Victoria basin. Basement and weathered-zone aquifers of this kind generally support community-scale boreholes but with yields that vary sharply over short distances.

findings.title: WHO — water, sanitation and hygiene topic guidance
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — WHO's WASH guidance covers drinking-water quality, sanitary protection of sources and the health burden of contaminated supplies. Densely settled lakeside and peri-urban areas with shallow water tables and on-site sanitation are the classic setting for the source-contamination pathways this guidance addresses.

findings.title: UNICEF — WASH programming
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — UNICEF runs long-standing WASH programmes across Kenya covering water supply for schools, health facilities and underserved communities. Its programme framing consistently identifies rapidly growing peri-urban fringes as areas where service expansion lags settlement growth.

findings.title: World Bank — Water global practice
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — The World Bank's water portfolio includes urban and rural water-supply investment and utility-strengthening operations in Kenya. Kisumu is a regional urban centre with an established utility and trunk road network, which generally lowers mobilisation difficulty for construction compared with remote rural sites.

findings.title: FAO AQUASTAT — water resources information
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — AQUASTAT compiles national water-resource and withdrawal statistics, including renewable resources and seasonality. Kenya's bimodal rainfall regime means supply schemes must be sized for inter-seasonal variability rather than for annual averages alone.

population.methodLabel: 1,155,574 reported residents of Kisumu (2019), OpenStreetMap, split by this site's share of mapped buildings (281 of 4,000 in the analysis area).
limitations: The published population figure covers the whole of Kisumu, City of Kisumu, Kisumu, Kenya; distributing it by building count assumes household size is uniform across the settlement.
OpenStreetMap building coverage is uneven, so a well-mapped neighbourhood is credited with a larger share than a poorly mapped one of the same size.
Neighbour counts are measured within 400 m of the site and scaled by area to the 1000 m service radius; real settlement is not uniform.
Everyone inside the service radius is assumed to be able and willing to walk to the point; terrain, land tenure and social barriers are not modelled.

recommendation.label: Solar-powered borehole with storage and tap stands
rationale: Groundwater evidence score is 0.70, at or above the 0.55 threshold for committing to a new drilled borehole.
Solar resource is 6.031 kWh/m2/day, at or above the 4 kWh/m2/day needed for a solar pump to run without a fuel supply chain.
No usable water point is mapped nearby, so there is no existing asset to rehabilitate instead.

components.name: Borehole
components.detail: Drilled, cased and gravel-packed borehole in the 40-70 m depth band implied by the groundwater evidence score. Actual depth is known only after drilling.

components.name: Solar pumping
components.detail: 600 Wp PV array, controller and submersible pump against an assumed 55 m pumping head.

components.name: Storage
components.detail: 12,000 L tank, sized at 1 day(s) of demand for 590 people at 20 L/person/day.

components.name: Distribution
components.detail: 1,877 m of conceptual distribution pipeline feeding 3 tap stand(s).

components.name: Monitoring
components.detail: Flow and system-status sensors with remote reporting for post-handover verification.

cost.accessMultiplierReason: Site is 29 m from the nearest mapped road on gently sloping terrain — 2% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
assumptions: Order-of-magnitude planning ranges for pre-feasibility screening — not a quotation, tender price or bill of quantities.
Quantities are sized for approximately 590 people at the service level assumed by the upstream sizing step.
Access surcharge applied to the subtotal: x1.02. Site is 29 m from the nearest mapped road on gently sloping terrain — 2% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
Totals are rounded outward to the nearest $1,000 (low down, high up) to avoid implying precision the method does not have.
Excludes land acquisition, taxes and import duties, permitting fees, contingency, and all recurrent operation and maintenance costs.
All unit rates are taken unchanged from the project coefficient table (RWSN/UNICEF rural water supply cost benchmarking (planning range)).
Drilling priced against the "favourable" depth band (40-70 m), selected by a groundwater evidence score of 0.70. Actual depth is only known after drilling.
Solar array rated at 600 Wp; no diesel or grid backup is priced.

output.formula: sustainable pump rate 1,800-3,060 L/h x effective pumping hours (6.031 kWh/m2/day x 0.78 = 4.704 h) x operational efficiency 0.82 = 6,940-11,800 L/day
caveats: Desk-study planning figures only. Borehole yield in particular is not guaranteed by a desk study: the sustainable rate must be confirmed by a step-drawdown and constant-rate pumping test on the completed borehole.
People supported assumes 20 L/person/day (WHO/UNICEF JMP service-level guidance); real consumption varies with walking distance, queueing time and the alternatives available.
No allowance is made for livestock, irrigation, institutional or commercial demand, which routinely consume a large share of a rural water point's output.

Sustainable abstraction band is 1800-3600 L/h (RWSN/UNICEF rural water supply cost benchmarking (planning range)); the upper bound is credited only in proportion to the groundwater evidence score of 0.70.
Output falls on overcast days and during array or pump downtime; storage sized upstream is what carries the community through those gaps.

recommendation.coverageNote: An estimated 56,825-105,533 people live within the 1,000 m service radius, but one installation of this type can supply 347-590. The system is sized to its own sustainable yield; covering the full catchment would require multiple installations.
assumptions: Residents within the service radius: 1,155,574 reported residents of Kisumu (2019), OpenStreetMap, split by this site's share of mapped buildings (281 of 4,000 in the analysis area). (range 56,825-105,533).

An estimated 56,825-105,533 people live within the 1,000 m service radius, but one installation of this type can supply 347-590. The system is sized to its own sustainable yield; covering the full catchment would require multiple installations.
The published population figure covers the whole of Kisumu, City of Kisumu, Kisumu, Kenya; distributing it by building count assumes household size is uniform across the settlement.
OpenStreetMap building coverage is uneven, so a well-mapped neighbourhood is credited with a larger share than a poorly mapped one of the same size.
Neighbour counts are measured within 400 m of the site and scaled by area to the 1000 m service radius; real settlement is not uniform.
Everyone inside the service radius is assumed to be able and willing to walk to the point; terrain, land tenure and social barriers are not modelled.
Demand is taken as 20 L/person/day (WHO/UNICEF JMP service-level guidance).
Storage is sized at 1 day(s) of demand and bounded to 5,000-200,000 L, the practical range for a single community installation.
Solar array sized from hydraulic work against an assumed 55 m pumping head, taken as the mid-point of the 40-70 m depth band that the cost model prices.
Pipeline length (1,877 m) and tap-stand count (3) are a conceptual layout from the geospatial step, not a surveyed route.
Order-of-magnitude planning ranges for pre-feasibility screening — not a quotation, tender price or bill of quantities.
Quantities are sized for approximately 590 people at the service level assumed by the upstream sizing step.
Access surcharge applied to the subtotal: x1.02. Site is 29 m from the nearest mapped road on gently sloping terrain — 2% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
Totals are rounded outward to the nearest $1,000 (low down, high up) to avoid implying precision the method does not have.
Excludes land acquisition, taxes and import duties, permitting fees, contingency, and all recurrent operation and maintenance costs.
All unit rates are taken unchanged from the project coefficient table (RWSN/UNICEF rural water supply cost benchmarking (planning range)).
Drilling priced against the "favourable" depth band (40-70 m), selected by a groundwater evidence score of 0.70. Actual depth is only known after drilling.
Solar array rated at 600 Wp; no diesel or grid backup is priced.
requiredValidation: Hydrogeological review and ground geophysical survey (resistivity or TEM) at the shortlisted point before any commitment.
Exploratory drilling with lithological logging and step-drawdown plus constant-rate pumping tests to establish sustainable yield.
Water-quality testing against national and WHO standards, including bacteriological, fluoride, arsenic, nitrate and salinity.
Land ownership confirmation and legal right of access or easement for the site and the pipeline corridor.
Community consultation on siting, tariff, and the operation and maintenance model, including who holds the spares.
Seasonal access verification — confirm the approach is passable for rigs and delivery vehicles in the wet season.
Environmental and social review, including abstraction licensing and downstream or aquifer impact.
Final engineering design, bill of quantities and competitive tender.

narrative: A solar-powered borehole in Kisumu can supply 347 to 590 people daily with 6,940 to 11,800 liters of water. Estimated costs range from $62,000 to $139,000 with 75% suitability and 66% confidence. These pre-feasibility estimates require field validation.
